label: Claude Fable 5.2
output:
Kelechi,

You said if I was serious I should put it in writing. A proper letter, not a voice note. So here is your proper letter, with a stamp on it, travelling from Peckham to Croydon like it's 1994. I hope you're reading it on the train like you promised.

I meant what I said at my birthday. You should come and teach maths. I wasn't just talking because there was cake.

Let me start with the bad parts, because I know you. If I only give you the sweet side, you'll fold this paper and use it as a bookmark.

Teaching is hard. The marking is endless. You finish one pile and another one has grown behind it. Some days the behaviour is pure wahala, and you go home having taught nothing to anybody, wondering why you ever left a quiet office where nobody argues with you about a seating plan. When I started in 2019, I cried in the car park twice in my first term. I'm not hiding that from you. It gets better, and I mean it properly gets better, but that first term humbled me.

And the money. The route I'm talking about is the salaried one, so you'd be paid while you train. It's one year, starting September 2027, and you're in a school from the beginning. But the pay in that first year is a drop from what you're on now. I won't dress it up. After that it goes up, there's a real pension, and there are the holidays, which I know you already envy because you complain about them every August.

So that's the worst of it. Now let me tell you about Damola.

Damola is in my Year 11 class. Last month we did simultaneous equations for three weeks, and for three weeks this boy looked at me like I was speaking Greek. Then one Tuesday something clicked. He solved one, checked it, looked up and shouted "Is that all??" across the room. The whole class clapped for him. I had to turn and face the board for a second.

That's the job, Kelechi. Not every day, but often enough. I honestly can't think of one thing in your spreadsheet that has ever made a room clap.

And you already know how to do this. That's what vexes me. You got an A in further maths. You were the one tutoring half our hostel in Moremi before exams, and people who had given up on themselves were passing because of you. At Christmas you taught my nephew fractions with jollof rice portions on plates, and he is still talking about it. He asked me last week when Uncle Kelechi is coming back. Nobody has ever asked when I'm coming back, and I do this for a living.

You're patient and you're funny, and you explain things without making the other person feel stupid. I work with trained teachers who are still learning that last one. Kids would love you. They can smell who actually likes them and who is just getting through the hour, and you would like them, even the annoying ones. Especially the annoying ones, knowing you.

Meanwhile, what are you doing? Checking other people's costings. Nine years in the same firm, and by your own mouth every day is the same spreadsheet. You are wasting yourself, my friend. I say it with love, but I'm saying it.

On your last birthday you told me, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." I didn't forget. You probably hoped I would.

Here is something that matters. My school has 1,100 kids, and two of our Year 9 maths groups have been covered by a supply teacher since September. These children are thirteen and fourteen, right at the age where they decide whether maths is for them or not, and nobody is staying long enough to learn their names. I'm not saying that to guilt you. I'm saying the need is real and it's ten minutes from where I'm sitting.

And before you start with "I'm too old to be changing career", a woman in my department started at 41 and she's one of the best we have. You're 34. If you start in September 2027, you'd have years of teaching behind you before 40 arrives. Or you can reach 40 at the same desk with the same spreadsheet. The birthday is coming either way.

I'm not asking you to resign or to sign anything. I'm asking for one evening.

The training partnership in Lewisham has an open evening on Thursday 19 November at 6pm. That's next week. Applications for next September open soon, so this is the right time to go and hear it from the people who run it, ask them your hard questions about the money, and see if the thing sits well with you. I'll come with you. If you hate it, you've lost one evening and I'll never raise it again. Okay, I'll raise it once more, at your next birthday, but gently.

If you don't hate it, then we talk properly.

You asked for it in writing, so you can't say you never got it. Thursday 19 November, 6pm, Lewisham. Text me yes and I'll meet you there.

Yours, and serious this time,

P.S. Yes, I posted it. Yes, I bought a stamp. That's how serious I am.

P.P.S. If you laugh at this on the train and people look at you, that's your business.

I left the sign-off without a name so you can sign it by hand after printing.
